# Module 1 — Full Test Bank {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note}
## How this test bank works
This bank holds **120 questions**. Section 1 gives you the data inside the question; Sections 2–4 each have ten questions for each of three datasets. On the real test you receive **four questions — one from each section — with the Section 2–4 questions all drawn from the same dataset**, and you submit an `.xlsx` workbook with **a separate sheet for each section's answers**. Each question is designed to take about **8–10 minutes**.

Expand each **Answer** block to check your work. Every value has been computed from the real data; when the source files are refreshed the exact numbers may shift slightly, but the method stays the same.
:::

**The three datasets.**

- **Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields** (1990–2025). Average yield (bu/ac) for eight crops in every Rural Municipality. Wide file `rm_yields_1990plus.csv` for Sections 2–3; long file `rm_yields_1990plus_long.csv` for Section 4. Blank = crop not grown/reported that RM-year. Lentils are recorded in **pounds** per acre, everything else in bushels.
- **Manitoba Wheat Variety** (2020–2025). Red spring wheat yield by variety and municipality, in `mb_wheat_varieties.csv`. `Reported = FALSE` marks a yield **suppressed** by MASC because too few farms grew that variety there.
- **Canada Field Crops** (Statistics Canada, 2015–2025). Seeded acres and average yield for major field crops by province, in `statcan_field_crops.csv`.

**Working with a single year.** Several questions ask you to work with one year of the data. Do **not** just apply a filter and point a formula at the whole column: as Module 1 explains, a filter hides rows from *you*, not from your formulas. Copy the rows you want onto a new sheet first, or use a conditional function that tests the year. If you copy 2023 out, you will have **295 rows** of data.

**Grading model.** **10%** for presentation — labelled cells, sensible formats, a reader can follow the sheet. The remaining **90%** is split evenly across the four questions, and evenly across the parts within each question. Parts are marked on **follow-through**: if an early part is wrong but the later parts are correctly worked *from your own earlier answer*, the later parts still earn full marks.

> **Vocabulary note.** Everything here uses only Module 1 tools: `SUM`, `AVERAGE`, `COUNT`, `COUNTA`, `MEDIAN`, `MODE.SNGL`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `ROUND`, `SUMPRODUCT`, `STDEV.S`, `VAR.S`, `QUARTILE.INC`, `PERCENTILE.INC`, `IF`, `COUNTIF`, `SUMIF`, `AVERAGEIF`, `XLOOKUP`; relative and absolute references; number and date formatting; sorting and filtering; wide vs long shape; and PivotTables.

---

# Section 1 — Building a Worksheet

*These questions are about spreadsheet mechanics: anchoring references, formatting numbers and dates, and order of operations. The data is given in the question — copy the block and paste it into Excel.*

### Question 1

*Paste this block into a blank sheet.*

```{.plain}
Field	Acres	Yield (bu/ac)
North	120	41.2
South	240	38.6
Creek	95	44.8
Home	310	36.1
Rented	175	39.9
```

Off to the right of the table, in a column with nothing else in it, put the canola price **$14.20** in a single labelled cell.

**(a)** Add a **Revenue ($/ac)** column: each field's yield times the price cell. Write the formula once and fill it down. Format as currency with two decimals.

**(b)** Add a **Total revenue ($)** column: revenue per acre times that field's acres. Format with a thousands separator and no decimals.

**(c)** Under the table, use `SUM` to total the acres, the total bushels (yield × acres), and the total revenue.

**(d)** In a spare column, repeat the (a) formula *without* the `$` signs and fill it down all five rows. Label the block clearly as the incorrect version.

**(e)** Beside it, write one sentence saying what appears in those cells and why.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) With the price in `F1`: `=C2*$F$1` → $585.04, $548.12, $636.16, $512.62, $566.58.
- (b) `=D2*B2` → $70,204.80 · $131,548.80 · $60,435.20 · $158,912.20 · $99,151.50.
- (c) Acres **940**; bushels **36,637.5**; total revenue **$520,252.50**.
- (d) The unanchored version, filled down five rows.
- (e) The first row is right; every row below it returns **$0.00**, because the price reference walks down to `F2`, `F3`… which are empty. Excel treats an empty cell as zero here and reports no error, so the column simply fills with zeros.
</details>

### Question 2

*Paste this block into a blank sheet.*

```{.plain}
Field	Canola	Wheat	Barley
North	41.2	52.4	63.1
South	38.6	49.8	58.7
Creek	44.8	55.2	66.4
Home	36.1	47.3	61.9
Rented	39.9	51.0	60.2
```

Directly above the three yield columns, enter the prices in a single row: Canola **$14.20**, Wheat **$8.35**, Barley **$5.60**.

**(a)** To the right, build a revenue-per-acre block of the same shape. Write **one** formula in its top-left cell and fill it across and down to complete all fifteen cells.

**(b)** State the formula you used, and say which part of the price reference is locked and which is not.

**(c)** Under your revenue block, use `AVERAGE` to find the mean revenue per acre for each crop.

**(d)** Which crop gives the highest average revenue per acre, and by how much over the second-placed crop?

**(e)** A student anchors the price fully as `$B$1` instead. In one sentence, say what their wheat and barley columns would show and why nothing on the sheet would look broken.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) With prices in row 1 and the first yield in `B3`: `=B3*B$1`, filled across and down. Any layout works provided the price **row** is locked and the column is not.
- (b) Only the **row** is locked (`B$1`). Filling down must keep pointing at the price row; filling across must let the column move so each crop meets its own price.
- (c) Canola **$569.70**, Wheat **$427.02**, Barley **$347.54**.
- (d) **Canola**, by about **$142.69** over wheat (569.704 − 427.019 = 142.685; accept $142.68 or $142.69 — the difference lands exactly on a half-cent).
- (e) Every column would use the canola price, so wheat and barley revenues would be roughly 70% and 150% too high. The sheet still fills with plausible dollar figures, so nothing signals the error.
</details>

### Question 3

*Paste this block into a blank sheet.*

```{.plain}
Date	Crop	Tonnes
14 September 2026	Canola	42.5
18 September 2026	Canola	38.0
23 September 2026	Wheat	61.2
2 October 2026	Wheat	55.8
9 October 2026	Barley	47.3
```

**(a)** Make sure Excel has read the dates as **dates**, not text, and format them as `DD-MMM-YYYY` (e.g. 14-Sep-2026). Show tonnes to one decimal.

**(b)** Add a **Days since previous** column. Leave the first row blank. Make sure the results show as plain numbers.

**(c)** In one cell, compute the number of days from the first delivery to the last.

**(d)** Use `SUM` to total the tonnes, and `AVERAGE` to find the mean load size.

**(e)** In one sentence, explain why part (b) would fail if Excel had stored the dates as text rather than as dates.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Dates formatted `DD-MMM-YYYY`; tonnes `0.0`.
- (b) `=A3-A2` filled down → **4, 5, 9, 7** days. If the cell shows `04-Jan-1900` it inherited the date format; change it to Number.
- (c) `=A6-A2` = **25** days.
- (d) Total **244.8** tonnes; mean **48.96** tonnes.
- (e) Excel stores a date as a number, which is why subtracting two of them gives a count of days. Text cannot be subtracted, so the formula would return an error instead of a gap.
</details>

### Question 4

*Paste this block into a blank sheet.*

```{.plain}
Load	Protein
A	0.1342
B	0.1285
C	0.1401
D	0.1198
E	0.1356
```

**(a)** Copy the protein column into a second column. Format the first as **General** and the second as **Percentage with 2 decimals**. Label both with the format used.

**(b)** Under each column, compute the average with `AVERAGE`, formatting each the same way as the column above it.

**(c)** The two averages display differently but hold the same number. In a spare cell, write that value to four decimal places.

**(d)** The contract pays a premium on any load above 13.5% protein. Add a column using `IF` that returns `Yes` or `No`, and use `COUNTIF` to count how many qualify.

**(e)** A student writes `=IF(B2>13.5,"Yes","No")` and gets `No` for every load. In one sentence, explain the error.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) The same five values twice; only the format differs. General shows `0.1342`, `0.1285`…; Percentage shows `13.42%`, `12.85%`….
- (b) Both averages hold the same number. General shows the full `0.13164`; the percentage column shows `13.16%`.
- (c) **0.1316**.
- (d) `=IF(B2>0.135,"Yes","No")`; `=COUNTIF(D2:D6,"Yes")` = **2** (loads C and E).
- (e) The cells hold proportions, not percentages — 0.1342, not 13.42. Nothing is above 13.5, so every row returns `No`. Formatting a cell as a percentage does not change the stored value.
</details>

### Question 5

*Paste this block into a blank sheet.*

```{.plain}
Field	Acres	Yield (bu/ac)
North	120	41.2
South	240	38.6
Creek	95	44.8
Home	310	36.1
Rented	175	39.9
```

**(a)** Use `AVERAGE` to find the plain mean of the five yields.

**(b)** Add a **Bushels** column (yield × acres) and total it, along with the acres, using `SUM`.

**(c)** The farm's actual average yield is total bushels divided by total acres. Compute it. Format both averages to one decimal place.

**(d)** Compute the same figure a second way, in a single cell, using `SUMPRODUCT` over `SUM`.

**(e)** The two averages in (a) and (c) differ. In one or two sentences, say which one answers "what did this farm average across all its acres", and what the plain mean is treating as equally important.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) `=AVERAGE(C2:C6)` = **40.1** bu/ac.
- (b) `=B2*C2` filled down; acres **940**, bushels **36,637.5**.
- (c) `=D7/B7` = **39.0** bu/ac.
- (d) `=SUMPRODUCT(C2:C6,B2:B6)/SUM(B2:B6)` = **39.0** — the same number in one step.
- (e) The **weighted** average in (c) answers it, because it counts every bushel once regardless of which field grew it. The plain mean treats each *field* as equally important, so the 95-acre Creek field — the highest yielding of the five — counts as much as the 310-acre Home field, and pulls the answer up by about 1.1 bu/ac.
</details>

# Section 2 — Descriptive Statistics and Distributions

## Questions 11–20 · Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields

### Question 11

*Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset.*

Work with the **Canola** column for 2023 (copy the 2023 rows to a sheet of their own first -- see the note above).

**(a)** Compute the mean and the median canola yield.

**(b)** Compare the two values. What does the relationship between the mean and the median tell you about how yields were distributed across RMs that year, and about the low-yielding RMs in particular?

**(c)** Compute the standard deviation and the interquartile range (IQR) of the same column.

**(d)** The IQR ignores the most extreme RMs while the standard deviation does not. Given what you found in (b), explain which of these two spread measures you would trust more to describe a "typical" amount of variation across RMs, and why.

**(e)** A classmate uses the mean to describe "a typical RM." Do you think the mean or the median better represents a typical RM here? Justify your choice using your answers to (a)–(d).

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) mean ≈ 33.88, median ≈ 35.50 bu/ac.
- (b) The mean falls **below** the median → a left/low tail: a minority of RMs with unusually low yields (down to ~3 bu/ac) pull the mean beneath the median. Most RMs cluster higher.
- (c) SD ≈ 13.33 bu/ac; IQR ≈ 22.30 bu/ac (Q1 ≈ 22.60, Q3 ≈ 44.90).
- (d) The **IQR** is more robust to the low-yield tail; the SD is inflated by the extreme low RMs. Either defensible if tied to the skew.
- (e) The **median** — the mean is dragged down by the low tail. Credit for naming the median *and* connecting it to the skew.
</details>

### Question 12

*Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset.*

Still on `Year = 2023`, compare the **Canola** column and the **Barley** column.

**(a)** Compute the mean and standard deviation of each crop's yield.

**(b)** Compare the two standard deviations. If one crop's is larger, does that by itself prove its yields were "more variable" in a meaningful sense? Explain the trap in comparing raw standard deviations across two crops with different averages.

**(c)** Compute the coefficient of variation (CV) for each crop.

**(d)** Using the CVs, state which crop's yields were more variable *relative to their average*, and by how much in rough terms.

**(e)** Write one sentence, suitable for a farm newspaper, that correctly compares the variability of the two crops without misleading the reader.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Canola: mean ≈ 33.88, SD ≈ 13.33. Barley: mean ≈ 54.56, SD ≈ 24.60.
- (b) No — barley also has a much higher mean, so a bigger SD is partly just scale. Comparing raw SDs across crops with different means is the trap.
- (c) CV = SD/mean. Canola ≈ 0.39; Barley ≈ 0.45.
- (d) Barley is **slightly** more variable relative to its mean (0.45 vs 0.39) — a modest difference.
- (e) e.g. "Relative to their average yields, Saskatchewan barley yields in 2023 were a little more variable than canola (CV 0.45 vs 0.39)."
</details>

### Question 13

*Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset.*

Compare **Canola** yields in a normal year and a drought year: filter first to `Year = 2019`, then to `Year = 2021`.

**(a)** Compute the mean and median canola yield for each of the two years.

**(b)** Compute the standard deviation and CV for each year.

**(c)** The CV is much higher in one of these years. Identify which, and explain in plain language what a higher CV means about how RMs fared relative to each other that year.

**(d)** Explain why a drought might make yields not just *lower* on average but also *more variable* across RMs (think about which RMs get rain and which don't).

**(e)** Which single year would you call "more predictable" for a canola grower, and which statistic supports that?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) 2019: mean ≈ 40.78, median ≈ 42.10. 2021: mean ≈ 21.86, median ≈ 22.80 bu/ac.
- (b) 2019: SD ≈ 8.17, CV ≈ 0.20. 2021: SD ≈ 8.14, CV ≈ 0.37.
- (c) **2021** has the far higher CV — relative to a low average, RMs differed a lot; some did much better or worse than others.
- (d) In drought, localized rain matters more — RMs that caught a storm did okay, those that missed it failed, widening the spread relative to the (low) mean.
- (e) **2019** is more predictable — its much lower CV (0.20 vs 0.37) shows tighter relative variation.
</details>

### Question 14

*Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset.*

Work with the **Oats** column for 2023 (copy the 2023 rows to a sheet of their own first -- see the note above).

**(a)** Compute the mean, median, and the 90th percentile of oat yield.

**(b)** State in plain language what the 90th percentile value tells you about RMs that year.

**(c)** Compute Q1, Q3, and the IQR.

**(d)** Compute the mean and median. Compare them and describe the shape of the distribution in Module-1 terms.

**(e)** Compare the IQR you found in (c) to the mean from (a) by computing the ratio IQR ÷ mean. Explain what a large value of this ratio tells you about how spread out oat yields were relative to their typical level.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) mean ≈ 71.14, median ≈ 75.90, P90 ≈ 116.72 bu/ac.
- (b) 90% of reporting RMs yielded ~117 bu/ac or less; only the top 10% exceeded it.
- (c) Q1 ≈ 44.98, Q3 ≈ 96.50, IQR ≈ 51.52 bu/ac.
- (d) Mean (71.1) below median (75.9) → slight left/low skew.
- (e) IQR ÷ mean ≈ 51.52 / 71.14 ≈ 0.72 — the middle-50% spread is nearly three-quarters of the typical yield, a large relative spread: RMs differed widely compared with the average level.
</details>

### Question 15

*Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset.*

Work with the **Flax** column for 2015 (copy the 2015 rows to a sheet of their own first -- see the note above).

**(a)** Compute the mean, median, standard deviation, and CV.

**(b)** Flax has a lower average yield than most other crops. Explain why comparing flax's standard deviation directly against, say, barley's would be misleading, and what statistic fixes that.

**(c)** Compute the range (max − min).

**(d)** Explain why the range is a fragile measure of spread compared with the IQR, using this column as an example.

**(e)** If you had to report a single "typical flax yield" and a single "typical spread" for 2015, which two statistics would you choose, and why?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) mean ≈ 23.62, median ≈ 23.64, SD ≈ 5.62, CV ≈ 0.238.
- (b) Flax's mean is low, so a small SD is expected on scale alone; the **CV** (SD/mean) compares relative variability fairly across crops.
- (c) range ≈ 40.15 − 4.25 ≈ 35.9 bu/ac.
- (d) The range depends on only the two most extreme RMs, so one unusual value swings it; the IQR uses the middle 50% and is stable.
- (e) **Median** (≈23.6) for centre and **IQR** (≈7.0) for spread — both resist extreme values. (Mean/SD acceptable given the near-symmetry, if justified.)
</details>

### Question 16

*Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset.*

Work with the **Durum** column for 2021, a drought year (copy the 2021 rows to a sheet of their own first).

**(a)** Compute the mean and median durum yield.

**(b)** The mean sits above the median this time. Describe the shape this implies, and contrast it with the left-skew seen in the 2023 canola data.

**(c)** Compute the CV.

**(d)** This is one of the highest CVs of any crop-year in the dataset. Explain, in terms a grower would understand, what such a high CV says about the 2021 durum crop across RMs.

**(e)** Explain why, in a year like this, quoting only the *mean* durum yield to describe the province would hide something important — and what you would add to tell the fuller story.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) mean ≈ 21.69, median ≈ 17.20 bu/ac.
- (b) Mean **above** median → a right/high tail (a minority of RMs did much better than the struggling majority) — the mirror image of the 2023 canola left-skew.
- (c) CV ≈ 0.57.
- (d) Enormous relative spread — RMs' fortunes diverged sharply; some near-failed while others were only moderately hit.
- (e) The mean alone hides that most RMs were *below* it (right-skew) and that spread was huge — add the median and the CV/IQR to show the typical RM did worse than the average suggests.
</details>

### Question 17

*Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset.*

Compare **Spring Wheat** and **Peas** for 2023, using the 2023 rows you extracted.

**(a)** Compute the mean and standard deviation of each.

**(b)** Compute the CV of each.

**(c)** The two CVs are similar. Explain what it means for two crops with very different average yields to have similar CVs.

**(d)** Compute the median of each and compare it to the mean. Do both crops show the same direction of skew?

**(e)** A student concludes "wheat and peas are equally risky to grow." Explain one thing this CV comparison does, and one thing it does not, support about that claim.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Spring Wheat: mean ≈ 42.87, SD ≈ 17.22. Peas: mean ≈ 33.96, SD ≈ 13.19.
- (b) Spring Wheat CV ≈ 0.40; Peas CV ≈ 0.39.
- (c) Their yields vary by a similar *proportion* of their own averages, even though wheat yields more in absolute bu/ac.
- (d) Wheat: mean < median (left skew). Peas: mean ≈ median (roughly symmetric). Not the same.
- (e) Supports: similar *relative yield variability*. Does not support: "risk" also depends on price, cost, and market — not shown here.
</details>

### Question 18

*Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset.*

Work with the **Canola** column across **all years** (do not filter by year).

**(a)** Compute the overall mean and median canola yield for 1990–2025.

**(b)** Compute the overall (all-years pooled) standard deviation.

**(c)** Now compute the standard deviation *within* just 1995 and within just 2023 (filter to each year). Compare these two within-year SDs to the pooled SD from (b), and note whether the pooled value falls above, below, or between them.

**(d)** Compute the average canola yield for `Year = 1995` and for `Year = 2020` separately. Using just these two numbers, describe how much average canola yield changed between an early and a recent year.

**(e)** Based on what you found in (d), explain why an overall 1990–2025 mean is a poor description of what a grower should expect in a recent year.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) mean ≈ 28.29, median ≈ 26.90 bu/ac (as of snapshot).
- (b) pooled SD ≈ 10.06 bu/ac.
- (c) Within-year SDs: 1995 ≈ 4.48 (tight), 2023 ≈ 13.33 (wide). The pooled SD (10.06) falls **between** them — early years were tightly clustered, recent drought-affected years spread out more, and pooling all years lands in the middle. (So a pooled SD is not automatically larger than every within-year SD.)
- (d) 1995 canola averages ≈ 19.2 vs 2020 ≈ 38.2 bu/ac — roughly double; average yields rose markedly from the mid-1990s to recent years.
- (e) Because recent years read much higher than early ones, a 36-year average (~28) sits well below recent levels and understates a recent-year expectation.
</details>

### Question 19

*Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset.*

Work with the **Barley** column for 2023 (copy the 2023 rows to a sheet of their own first -- see the note above).

**(a)** Compute Q1, Q3, and the IQR.

**(b)** Using the 1.5×IQR rule, compute the lower and upper "fences" (Q1 − 1.5·IQR and Q3 + 1.5·IQR).

**(c)** Count how many RMs (if any) fall outside those fences — i.e. would be flagged as outliers on a box plot.

**(d)** The minimum barley yield this year is about 2.9 bu/ac. Explain whether the 1.5×IQR rule flags it as an outlier, and why a genuinely low value might *not* be flagged when the spread is already very wide.

**(e)** Explain in one sentence why a wide IQR makes the outlier fences more forgiving.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Q1 ≈ 32.60, Q3 ≈ 74.00, IQR ≈ 41.40 bu/ac.
- (b) Lower fence ≈ 32.60 − 62.10 ≈ −29.5; upper ≈ 74.00 + 62.10 ≈ 136.1.
- (c) **Zero** RMs fall outside — even the ~2.9 min is above −29.5.
- (d) The min (2.9) is above the lower fence, so it is **not** flagged; the very wide IQR (41.4) pushes the fence far below any real value.
- (e) A wider IQR makes 1.5×IQR larger, so the fences sit farther from the quartiles and catch fewer points.
</details>

### Question 20

*Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset.*

Work with the **Spring Wheat** column and compare `Year = 2015` with `Year = 2019` (two non-drought years).

**(a)** Compute the mean and median spring wheat yield for each year.

**(b)** Compute the standard deviation and CV for each year.

**(c)** State which year had the higher average, and whether the higher-average year was also more or less variable in relative terms.

**(d)** Explain why two "good" years can still differ noticeably in average yield (name one factor).

**(e)** Describe, in one sentence, how you would summarise the *difference* between these two years to a non-technical reader using the statistics you computed.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) 2015: mean ≈ 37.02, median ≈ 37.49. 2019: mean ≈ 49.23, median ≈ 50.05 bu/ac.
- (b) 2015: SD ≈ 8.67, CV ≈ 0.234. 2019: SD ≈ 11.11, CV ≈ 0.226.
- (c) 2019 is higher on average (~12 bu/ac more); its CV (0.226) is about equal to 2015's (0.234), so it was **not** more variable in relative terms.
- (d) Growing-season weather differs year to year even between two good years (rainfall timing, heat, frost). Any sensible factor credited.
- (e) e.g. "2019 spring wheat yielded about 12 bu/ac more than 2015 on average, with similar relative variability across RMs."
</details>

## Questions 21–30 · Manitoba Wheat Variety

### Question 21

*Using the Manitoba Wheat Variety dataset.*

Work with the **reported** yields only (`Reported = TRUE`).

**(a)** Compute the mean and the median of the reported yields.

**(b)** Compare the two values, and describe in Module-1 terms what their relationship implies about the shape of the yield distribution.

**(c)** Compute the standard deviation, the IQR, and the coefficient of variation.

**(d)** The CV for Saskatchewan 2023 canola was about 0.39. Compare it to the CV you found here and interpret the contrast in one sentence a grower would understand.

**(e)** Based only on the shape and the CV you computed, would you describe this dataset as more or less consistent than the Saskatchewan 2023 canola data? Point to the specific numbers that justify your answer.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) mean ≈ 61.16, median ≈ 62.20 bu/ac.
- (b) Mean ≈ median → **roughly symmetric**, unlike the left-skewed SK canola.
- (c) SD ≈ 12.38, IQR ≈ 15.70, CV ≈ 0.20.
- (d) CV ≈ 0.20 vs ≈ 0.39 — e.g. "these wheat yields vary about half as much, relative to their average, as SK canola did in 2023."
- (e) **More consistent** — justified by the lower CV (0.20 vs 0.39) and the roughly symmetric shape (mean ≈ median) versus the SK left skew. Answer must cite the numbers, not outside reasoning.
</details>

### Question 22

*Using the Manitoba Wheat Variety dataset.*

Continue with the reported yields.

**(a)** Compute the 90th percentile of the reported yields and state, in plain language, what it means.

**(b)** Compute the minimum reported yield.

**(c)** Compute how many standard deviations the minimum sits below the mean (that is, (mean − minimum) ÷ SD). Explain what this distance tells you about how extreme the lowest value is.

**(d)** Explain what would happen to the mean, versus the median, if that single lowest value were removed — and why the two measures respond differently to one extreme value.

**(e)** Which single number — mean or median — would you headline in a report titled "typical Manitoba wheat yield," and why?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) P90 ≈ 75.8 bu/ac — 90% of reported results were at or below this.
- (b) minimum ≈ 4.5 bu/ac.
- (c) (61.16 − 4.5) / 12.38 ≈ 4.6 standard deviations below the mean — a very extreme low value, far outside the bulk of the data.
- (d) Removing it would raise the **mean** noticeably (mean sums every value) but barely move the **median** (a position).
- (e) The **median** — not distorted by the low extreme, so it better represents "typical."
</details>

### Question 23

*Using the Manitoba Wheat Variety dataset.*

Filter the reported yields to a single year, `Year = 2021`, and then to `Year = 2023`.

**(a)** Compute the mean and median reported yield for each of the two years.

**(b)** Compute the standard deviation and CV for each year.

**(c)** 2021 was a drought year on the Prairies. State whether the Manitoba variety data shows a lower average that year, and by roughly how much.

**(d)** Compare the CVs of the two years and say whether the drought year was also *more variable* in relative terms.

**(e)** The Saskatchewan RM canola CV was about 0.37 in the 2021 drought, while this Manitoba wheat CV stayed near 0.25. Using only these numbers, state which dataset's yields were disturbed *more* by the drought in relative terms.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) 2021: mean ≈ 49.64, median ≈ 50.55. 2023: mean ≈ 61.42, median ≈ 61.90 bu/ac. (2021 lower.)
- (b) 2021: SD ≈ 12.20, CV ≈ 0.246. 2023: SD ≈ 11.27, CV ≈ 0.184.
- (c) Yes — 2021 averages ~12 bu/ac below 2023, a clear drought drop.
- (d) 2021's CV (0.246) is noticeably higher than 2023's (0.184) — the drought year was more variable in relative terms, though both stay well below SK field CVs.
- (e) The **Saskatchewan** data was disturbed more in relative terms — its drought-year CV (~0.37) is much higher than the Manitoba figure (~0.25), so its yields spread out more relative to their average.
</details>

**(c)** Explain the difference between this problem and the problem of pooling many *provinces* into one national average — i.e. pooling *crops* vs pooling *places*. Both blend unlike things into one number; describe what each one hides.

### Question 34

*Using the Canada Field Crops dataset.*

**(b)** Compute the CV of each.

**(c)** State which crop is more variable in relative terms across the country, and cite the two CVs that justify your answer.

**(d)** Barley and soybeans have almost identical standard deviations, yet very different CVs. Explain how that is possible.

**(e)** A student says "barley and soybeans are equally variable because their standard deviations are the same." Using your CV results, explain what is wrong with that claim.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Barley: mean ≈ 64.24, SD ≈ 9.10. Soybeans: mean ≈ 39.56, SD ≈ 9.08.
- (b) Barley CV ≈ 0.142; Soybeans CV ≈ 0.229.
- (c) **Soybeans** are more variable in relative terms — CV 0.229 vs 0.142.
- (d) The SDs are nearly equal (~9.1), but barley's mean (64) is much higher than soybeans' (40); dividing the same SD by a bigger mean gives a smaller CV. Relative variability depends on the mean, not the SD alone.
- (e) Equal SDs describe equal *absolute* spread, but relative to their different averages soybeans vary much more (CV 0.23 vs 0.14). "Equally variable" ignores that the two crops have very different mean yields.
</details>

# Section 3 — Conditional Functions & Lookups

## Questions 41–50 · Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields

### Question 41

*Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset.*

Use the full (all-years) dataset.

**(a)** Use `AVERAGEIF` to find the average canola yield in each of 2010, 2019, and 2021.

**(b)** Rank those three years by average yield, and identify which one stands out as unusually low.

**(c)** For each of the same three years, describe what you would check across the *other* crop columns to decide whether the low year was a broad event affecting all crops, rather than a canola-only result. (You do not need outside knowledge — describe the data check.)

**(d)** Your `AVERAGEIF` for 2023 returns a number even though several RMs have a blank canola cell that year. Explain what `AVERAGEIF` did with those blanks.

**(e)** Explain why filling those blanks with 0 before averaging would give a wrong answer.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) 2010 ≈ 29.82, 2019 ≈ 40.78, 2021 ≈ 21.86 bu/ac. `=AVERAGEIF(A:A, 2021, E:E)`.
- (b) 2019 highest, 2010 middle, **2021** lowest — the standout.
- (c) Compute each other crop's `AVERAGEIF` for 2021 and see whether they are *also* low; if every crop's 2021 average is depressed, the low year is broad, not canola-specific.
- (d) `AVERAGEIF` **skips blank cells**, averaging only the RMs that reported.
- (e) Filling blanks with 0 counts "no data" as "a yield of zero," dragging the average down artificially.
</details>

### Question 42

*Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset.*

**(a)** Use `COUNTIF` to count how many RM-year rows have a canola yield above 40 bu/ac across all years.

**(b)** Use `COUNT` to find how many non-blank canola cells there are in total.

**(e)** Explain why the proportion in (c) describes *reported* RM-years only, and why that is a limitation if some years have many blanks.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) ≈ 1483 rows. `=COUNTIF(E:E, ">40")`.
- (b) ≈ 10,039 non-blank canola cells. `=COUNT(E:E)`.
- (c) ≈ 1483 / 10039 ≈ **0.148** — about 15% of reported RM-years had canola above 40 bu/ac.
- (d) Above 50 the count falls to ≈181 — most canola yields sit well below 50, so raising the bar excludes the bulk of the distribution.
- (e) It is computed only over cells that have data; years with many blank RMs contribute fewer rows, so the proportion reflects reported RM-years, not all RM-years.
</details>

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (b) ≈ 52.9 bu/ac.

- (d) The RM-year combination may not exist in the data, or that crop's cell for that RM-year may be blank (crop not grown/reported).

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (d) `COUNTIFS` counts rows where conditions co-occur in the same record; separate `COUNTIF`s only count each condition independently and cannot tell you how often they happen together.
- (e) "A alone" counts any row passing A; "A and B" counts only rows passing both at once — always fewer or equal.

**(b)** State which RM has the higher long-run average barley yield, and by roughly how much.

**(c)** Use `COUNT` (via a helper or `COUNTIF` on the RM) to find how many years each RM reports barley. Explain why comparing the two averages is fair only if both rest on a similar number of years.

**(d)** Explain why an `AVERAGEIF` on RM gives a *per-RM* average, whereas an `AVERAGEIF` on Year gives a *per-year* average — and why you must be clear which you are reporting.

**(e)** State, in one sentence, what "average barley yield in RM 1" means in words.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) RM 1 ≈ 56.56 bu/ac; RM 100 ≈ 43.89 bu/ac. `=AVERAGEIF(B:B, 1, F:F)`.
- (b) RM 1 is higher by ≈ 12.7 bu/ac.
- (c) Each reports ~35 years, so the comparison is fair; if one had far fewer years it could reflect a different set of (e.g. good or bad) years.
- (d) `AVERAGEIF` on RM averages all years for one RM; on Year it averages all RMs for one year — different groupings answering different questions.
- (e) It is the mean barley yield in RM 1 taken over all the years that RM reported barley.
</details>

### Question 46

*Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset.*

**(a)** Use `COUNTIF` with a computed threshold to count how many canola cells (all years) are above the *overall* average canola yield. First compute the overall average with `AVERAGE`, then use `">"&` that average as the `COUNTIF` criterion.

**(b)** Report both the overall average and the count above it.

**(c)** Roughly what fraction of reported canola cells are above the mean? Explain whether you would expect this fraction to be exactly one-half.

**(d)** Explain why, for a left-skewed distribution, *more* than half the values can sit above the mean.

**(e)** Explain why you cannot write the criterion as `">AVERAGE(E:E)"` in quotes, and must use `">"&AVERAGE(E:E)` instead.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) `=COUNTIF(E:E, ">"&AVERAGE(E:E))`.
- (b) overall average ≈ 28.29 bu/ac; count above ≈ 4519.
- (c) ≈ 4519 / 10039 ≈ 0.45 — a bit **below** half, not exactly one-half.
- (d) In a left-skewed set the low tail pulls the mean down, so a majority can sit above it; here the pooled multi-decade data behaves differently, and the fraction lands near 0.45 — the point is that "above the mean" need not be 50%.
- (e) Quoted, `">AVERAGE(E:E)"` is treated as literal text; `">"&AVERAGE(E:E)` concatenates the ">" with the computed number to build a real numeric criterion.
</details>

### Question 47

*Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset.*

**(d)** Explain why comparing absolute changes between two crops with different typical yields can be misleading, and what you could divide by to compare fairly.

**(e)** State, in one sentence, the difference between an absolute change (bu/ac) and a relative change (percent).

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Canola: 2015 ≈ 36.06, 2019 ≈ 40.78 bu/ac.
- (b) Barley: 2015 ≈ 55.25, 2019 ≈ 68.59 bu/ac.
- (c) Canola rose ≈ 4.7; barley rose ≈ 13.3 — **barley** rose more in absolute bu/ac.
- (d) Barley yields more to begin with, so a larger absolute rise is partly scale; divide the change by the starting value to get a percent change for a fair comparison.
- (e) Absolute change is the raw bu/ac difference; relative change expresses that difference as a fraction of the starting value.
</details>

### Question 48

*Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset.*

**(a)** Write an `IF` (or `IFS`) formula that labels each RM-year's canola yield as `"Low"` (below 20), `"Medium"` (20 to 40), or `"High"` (above 40), leaving blanks blank.

**(b)** Use `COUNTIF` to count how many cells fall in each of the three labels.

**(c)** Which label is most common? Relate that to the overall average canola yield (~28 bu/ac).

**(d)** Explain how you would modify the formula to avoid labelling a blank cell as "Low."

**(e)** State, in one sentence, why an explicit label column can be more useful for a reader than the raw numbers alone.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) `=IF(E2="", "", IFS(E2<20,"Low",E2<=40,"Medium",TRUE,"High"))`.
- (b) Count each label with `=COUNTIF(label_range, "Medium")`, etc.
- (c) "Medium" (20–40) is most common, consistent with the ~28 bu/ac average sitting inside that band.
- (d) Wrap the classification in `IF(E2="", "", …)` so blank inputs return blank, not "Low."
- (e) Labels group the data into meaningful bands a reader can scan quickly, without interpreting every raw number.
</details>

**(b)** State which crop is reported in more RM-years, and by roughly how much.

**(d)** Explain why you would use `COUNT` (numbers only) rather than `COUNTA` (any non-empty cell) here.

**(e)** State, in one sentence, why the count of reported cells is itself a useful summary, separate from the average yield.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Canola ≈ 10,039; Flax ≈ 8,077 non-blank cells. `=COUNT(E:E)`, `=COUNT(J:J)`.
- (b) Canola is reported in more RM-years, by ≈ 1,960.
- (c) Canola has more reported cells, so it is recorded in more RM-years than flax across the 1990–2025 span.
- (d) `COUNT` counts numeric entries only; `COUNTA` would also count any stray text, giving a misleading total.
- (e) It measures data coverage — how widely the crop is recorded — which the average yield does not capture.
</details>

### Question 50

*Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset.*

**(a)** Use `AVERAGEIF` to compute the average canola yield for the year 2021 and for 2023.

**(b)** Use `COUNTIFS` to count, within 2021 only, how many RMs had canola below 20 bu/ac.

**(c)** Use `COUNTIFS` to do the same for 2023.

**(d)** Compare the two counts and explain what the difference says about how the two years differed at the low end.

**(e)** Explain, in one sentence, why comparing counts below a fixed threshold across two years is a fair way to describe how bad the worse year was.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) 2021 ≈ 21.86; 2023 ≈ 33.88 bu/ac. `=AVERAGEIF(A:A, 2021, E:E)`.
- (b) 2021 below 20: `=COUNTIFS(A:A, 2021, E:E, "<20")` — a large count (roughly a third of RMs).
- (c) 2023 below 20: far fewer RMs.
- (d) Many more RMs fell below 20 bu/ac in 2021 than 2023, showing 2021's low end was far worse — a broad poor year.
- (e) A fixed threshold gives a common yardstick, so the count of RMs beneath it directly compares how many did badly in each year.
</details>

## Questions 51–60 · Manitoba Wheat Variety

### Question 51

*Using the Manitoba Wheat Variety dataset.*

**(a)** Use `COUNTIF` on the `Reported` column to count the suppressed rows (`FALSE`) and the reported rows (`TRUE`).

**(b)** State which is larger.

**(c)** Divide the reported count by the total number of rows. Explain in plain language what that proportion represents.

**(d)** Explain what a suppressed row means in this dataset, and why it is a different kind of "missing" than a blank in the Saskatchewan file. (Describe the data meaning, not farming.)

**(e)** A student deletes all suppressed rows before analysing. Give one calculation that is unaffected by this, and one conclusion that would be biased by it.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) ≈ 2960 FALSE, ≈ 2398 TRUE. `=COUNTIF(G:G, "FALSE")`.
- (b) Suppressed (FALSE) is larger.
- (c) ≈ 2398 / 5358 ≈ **0.45** — about 45% of rows carry a published yield.
- (d) A suppressed row means the number was withheld (too few farms reported); a Saskatchewan blank means the crop was not grown/reported. One withholds a known value, the other has no value.
- (e) Unaffected: the average of reported yields (blanks are skipped anyway). Biased: any statement about how *widely* a variety is grown, since suppressed rows carry that coverage information.
</details>

- (d) ≈ 570 total appearances — every municipality-year where the variety was listed.

### Question 69

*Using the Canada Field Crops dataset.*

**(a)** Use `AVERAGEIF` to compute the average canola yield for each of 2019, 2021, and 2023 across provinces.

**(b)** Rank the three years and identify the lowest.

**(c)** Explain how comparing a single year's average to the others flags an unusual year — using the numbers only.

**(d)** Explain why the province-level average in the low year may not look as extreme as the RM-level average for the same year in the Saskatchewan data.

**(e)** State, in one sentence, why averaging up to the province level hides some of the variation the finer data shows.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Compute each with `AVERAGEIFS` (Crop = Canola, Year). 2021 is the low one.
- (b) 2021 lowest; 2019 and 2023 higher.
- (c) The low year's average sits clearly below the others, marking it as unusual without any outside information.
- (d) Each province figure is already an average over its farms, so within-province lows are smoothed before you see them.
- (e) Province averages combine many farms into one number, hiding the farm- or RM-level spread beneath them.
</details>

### Question 70

*Using the Canada Field Crops dataset.*

**(a)** Use `SUMIFS` to compute total spring wheat seeded acres in 2023, and use `AVERAGEIFS` to compute the average spring wheat yield in 2023.

**(b)** Explain, in words, why you cannot multiply your single average yield by your single total acreage to get exact national production.

**(c)** Explain what extra breakdown (by province) you would need to compute production correctly.

**(d)** Explain why a province with high yield but few acres contributes little to national production.

**(e)** State, in one sentence, the general relationship between a rate, a quantity, and a total (production = yield × acres, per province).

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Total seeded ≈ 19,496,400 acres; average yield computed with `AVERAGEIFS`.
- (b) The national average yield is a plain average across provinces, not weighted by acres, so average × total does not equal the true sum of province-level (yield × acres).
- (c) You need each province's own yield and acres, multiply within each province, then add those products.
- (d) Production = yield × acres per province; few acres means a small product regardless of a high yield.
- (e) For each province, production = yield × acres; national production is the sum of those province products, not the national average times national acres.
</details>

# Section 4 — PivotTables

## Questions 71–80 · Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields (long file)

### Question 72

*Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset (long file).*

**(a)** Build a PivotTable with Year on Rows and Crop on Columns (Yield as Average, Unit filtered to `bu/ac`).

**(b)** Compare canola in 2021 versus 2023, and describe the size of the change in plain language.

**(c)** Scan the 2021 row across all crops. Describe what you notice.

**(d)** Explain how a whole low *row* (a year) differs, in cause, from a single low *column* value (one crop in one year).

**(e)** State what the grid lets you conclude about 2021, and why.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Year × Crop grid of average yields.
- (b) Canola in 2021 (≈21.9) is about one-third lower than 2023 (≈33.9) — a large drop.
- (c) *Every* crop's 2021 average is low, not just canola.
- (d) A low row = a broad cause hitting all crops that year; a single low column value = a crop-specific problem that year.
- (e) 2021 was a broad, region-wide low year — the whole row is depressed, so the cause was general rather than crop-specific.
</details>

### Question 73

*Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset (long file).*

**(a)** Build a single PivotTable with Crop on Rows and Year on Columns (Yield as Average, Unit = bu/ac), then filter the columns to just 2019 and 2025.

**(b)** For each crop, read the 2019 and 2025 values and compute the change (2025 minus 2019).

**(c)** State which crop rose the most in absolute bu/ac between those two years.

**(d)** Explain why the crop that rose most in absolute terms is not necessarily the one that rose most in *relative* terms.

**(e)** Describe how you would use the PivotTable output to compute a relative change for each crop.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) One Crop × Year pivot, columns filtered to 2019 and 2025.
- (b) 2025 minus 2019 per crop (e.g. Oats 97.5 − 89.4 ≈ 8.1; Barley 72.8 − 68.6 ≈ 4.2; Canola 43.9 − 40.8 ≈ 3.1).
- (c) **Oats** rose most in absolute bu/ac (~8).
- (d) Oats already yield the most, so a big absolute gain can be a small percentage; a lower-yielding crop's smaller gain could be a larger percentage.
- (e) Divide each crop's change by its 2019 value to get the relative (percent) change.
</details>

### Question 74

*Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset (long file).*

**(a)** Build a PivotTable of the **count** of reporting RMs for canola each year (Crop filtered to Canola, Year on Rows, Yield as Count).

**(b)** State roughly how many RMs report canola in a typical recent year.

**(c)** Explain what a change in the yearly count would tell you about reporting coverage, using counts only.

**(d)** Explain why you would use Count (not Average) for this particular question.

**(e)** State, in one sentence, the difference between a PivotTable Count and a PivotTable Average of the same field.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Year on Rows, Yield → Values set to **Count**.
- (b) About **290** RMs report canola in recent years.
- (c) A stable count means steady coverage; a dip would signal fewer RMs reporting that year.
- (d) Count answers "how many RMs reported," whereas Average answers "what did they yield" — here you want the number of reports.
- (e) Count tallies how many values there are; Average gives their mean — one measures coverage, the other level.
</details>

### Question 75

*Using the Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields dataset (long file).*

**(d)** Explain how having Count next to Average in the same PivotTable helps you judge each average.

**(e)** State, in one sentence, why you would show both Average and Count when presenting a by-crop summary.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Crop on Rows; Yield → Average and Yield → Count.
- (b) Report the most- and fewest-reported crops from the count column (e.g. Spring Wheat/Barley high, Flax/Durum lower in 2023).
- (c) A crop with fewer reporting RMs has an average built on less data, so it is more easily swayed by a few RMs.
- (d) The count tells you how much data supports each average, so you know which averages to trust more.
- (e) The average states the level and the count states its support — together they let a reader weigh each figure.
</details>

- (b) Corn for grain highest (~136), then Oats (~79), Barley (~64) … down to Flax (~26).
- (c) Corn yields the most per acre, but a high per-acre yield says nothing about how many acres of corn are grown.
- (d) Pivot `Seeded_acres` as Sum by crop to see how much of each is planted.
- (e) The yield pivot ranks per-acre productivity; the acres pivot ranks scale — different questions.
</details>

### Question 98

- (d) Fewer reporting province-years means the national average is built from less data and covers less of the country.
- (e) The count shows how broadly a crop is reported, so you know how far its national average really extends.
</details>
